values.value: Why one open standard changed how agents and apps talk

value.markup: Welcome to the blog. These two posts argue the case for the Model Context Protocol (MCP): a small standard with an outsized effect on how AI agents reach the world around them. Grab a coffee and read on.

values.value: Why MCP Is Awesome: One Protocol, Every Tool
Before MCP, every AI integration was a bespoke plumbing job. One open protocol changed that — and the reasons it wins are simpler than you'd think.
One protocol, every tool — the end of bespoke integrations

value.markup:
Ask anyone who wired an AI agent up to real systems before the Model Context Protocol existed, and they will describe the same winter: an M × N problem. Every model had to be taught to speak to every tool, and every tool had to be taught to speak to every model. Each connection was hand-built, fragile, and doomed to be rebuilt.

MCP collapses that grid into a line. Ship one MCP server for your calendar, your CMS, your database — and any conforming client can use it. Write one MCP client, and it can reach every server anyone has ever published. The integration work goes from quadratic to linear, which is the kind of change that rewrites roadmaps.

values.value: Photo: Alexandre Debiève / Unsplash — the standard interface, in silicon form

value.markup:
The second reason MCP is awesome is less flashy but matters more: it is boring on purpose. It builds on JSON-RPC, it needs no special infrastructure, and it deliberately leaves model internals alone. Nothing in the protocol assumes a particular vendor, which means nobody has to ask permission to build on it — and nobody can take it away.

That combination — one open standard, zero vendor lock-in, linear integration cost — is why every serious AI platform now speaks it. When the plumbing becomes a commodity, the interesting work moves up the stack. That is exactly what MCP did.

values.value: MCP in Practice: The Site You Are Reading Right Now
This blog was modeled, populated and published through the Umbraco MCP server — a live demonstration of exactly what the first post praises.
The proof is the page you are reading

value.markup:
This site is not an illustration — it is a receipt. Every document type, every data type, every template and every piece of content you can see was created through the Umbraco MCP server: typed tool calls against a management API, no hand-editing, no migration scripts.

Notice what that felt like from the outside. The agent asked for a blog; the CMS exposed modeling as tools and the agent composed them — element types here, a block grid there, content snapped into the slots the schema defines. There was no scraping of a UI and no brittle macro recorder, because the protocol speaks in the CMS's own vocabulary.

values.value: Photo: Shubham Dhage / Unsplash — every block clicks into a slot the model knows about

value.markup:
And that is the quiet lesson of MCP: when the surface area between an agent and a system is precisely defined, the agent stops guessing. It reads the schema, follows the rules, and writes values that validate. The result you are reading was assembled block by block — hero, rich text, image — each one a protocol call, not a mouse click.

The tools did not make the agent smart. They made the agent grounded — and that is the part worth standardizing.
